# 14 Barbershop Marketing Ideas To Get More Clients

[Marcy Miniano](https://bookedin.com/blog/author/marcy/) February 13, 2026 14 minute read

These days, the way most clients find a new barbershop is online. In fact, [about **97%**](https://coolest-gadgets.com/google-my-business-statistics/) of people learn about local businesses through the internet. 

So if your schedule isn’t as full as you’d like, it doesn’t necessarily mean you’re doing anything wrong. Sometimes, it’s simply because not enough people know about your shop.

That’s where using the right marketing tactics comes in. We’ve rounded up 14 barbershop marketing ideas to help you [bring in new clients consistently](https://bookedin.com/blog/how-to-increase-barber-clientele/), stand out from nearby shops, and even [keep your profit margins](https://bookedin.com/blog/are-barbershops-profitable-what-to-know/) healthy.

Table of contents

## Barbershop Marketing Ideas To Help Your Business Grow & Succeed

Below are the most effective barbershop marketing ideas: some you can start as early as this week with no big budget needed, others are longer-term strategies you’ll need to put in more effort and budget into. 

**_Note:_** _Feeling overwhelmed or short on time? Skip ahead to the FAQ section for our take on what to do first._

### 1\. Make your Google Business Profile do the selling for you

> **_Effort & cost:_** _Long-term play; medium budget_

When someone searches for “barber near me” or “fade \[your city or neighborhood\]”, [you want your shop to be](https://bookedin.com/blog/barbershop-name-ideas/) part of the top results that people would see. 

This is why you should **optimize [your Google Business Profile](https://bookedin.com/blog/how-to-get-more-google-reviews-for-service-business/)**, since it’s where most potential clients would decide whether or not to book with you, based on the photos, service menu, ratings, distance, and hours. 

In fact, studies show that a fully completed profile gets [**7x** more clicks](https://searchendurance.com/google-business-profile-statistics/) than an incomplete one. Below are the steps for how to go about this:

*   Add **new, high-quality photos every other week** (a mix of before/after shots, shop interiors, team photos). It helps reassure people that your shop is very much active. 
*   Use **Google Business Profile Posts to promote offers, announcements, and events** (e.g., “Back-to-school cuts this weekend” or “Walk-ins open Sunday from 12:00 to 3:00 PM”).
*   Make sure that your **services, prices, and shop hours are always up to date**. 
*   Put a **link to your booking page**, so people can reserve a slot in just a few taps or clicks. 
*   Use the **Questions & Answers feature to proactively answer common questions**, such as “_Do you take walk-ins?_”, “_Do you do beards?_”, and “_Do you accept card/Apple Pay?_”. 

### 2\. Encourage clients to leave you a review on online directories

> _**Effort & cost:** Quick win; free_

It’s important that you get **a good amount of** [**positive reviews constantly**](https://bookedin.com/blog/how-to-get-client-customer-testimonials/) **on third-party platforms** like Google and Yelp. After all, reviews are one of the fastest ways to build your shop’s credibility. 

Ask happy clients (especially new ones) after their appointment, and hand them a small card with a QR code leading to the link where they can post their review. Alternatively, you can send them a thank-you text containing that link. 

Don’t forget to [**respond to reviews**](https://bookedin.com/blog/how-to-respond-negative-reviews/)**, whether they’re good or bad**. That way, other people will see that you’re professional and your shop is very much active. 

Lastly, a small but important warning: **Don’t offer discounts or freebies in exchange for reviews**. Most platforms (Google included) strongly forbid incentives for reviews and may even restrict profiles that do such a thing. 

### 3\. Set up a barbershop website that includes a 24/7 booking page

> _**Effort & cost:** Long-term play; medium budget_

Think of your website as your shop’s online storefront: It’s where many people would go when they want to know what you offer, why they should choose you over other barbershops, whether you’re legit, and how to book an appointment with you. 

That’s why your barbershop website **should be super easy to navigate and mobile-friendly**, so a first-time visitor can quickly find your services, pricing, location, hours, and even photos of your work. 

Your website should also **include a built-in booking page or widget** that makes it easy for visitors to pick a service, choose a time, and reserve their slot — without having to switch to a different tab just to contact you. 

> **Tip:** If you’re using Bookedin, you can [add a Bookedin button](https://support.bookedin.com/hc/en-us/articles/201792883-Website-Booking-Button) on your site instead of just a booking page link! You can also [embed your appointment calendar](https://support.bookedin.com/hc/en-us/articles/207656763-Website-booking-calendar) so people immediately see which dates are available.  

[Book a free demo to explore all features](https://bookedin.com/book-a-demo/)

### 4\. Post social media content that shows results

> _**Effort & cost:** Ongoing effort; free or low cost_

Your social media pages should feel like a portfolio, not just a bulletin board for announcements. This is especially true [for your shop’s Instagram](https://bookedin.com/blog/how-to-turn-instagram-followers-into-clients/) and TikTok.

Make it a point to **regularly** **post the kind of content that would make someone think, “****_Yes, I’m choosing this shop_****.”**

Here are some ideas for **useful and proof-based** social media content you should try out (if you haven’t yet): 

*   Before-and-after transformations using the same angle and good lighting
*   10-20 second Reels showcasing your precision work (i.e., edges sharp, fade smooth)
*   “What to ask for” videos that help people explain what they want (e.g., “Low taper vs. mid fade”)
*   Introductions of yourself and/or your team of barbers 
*   Client reaction videos when they see the results they’ve gotten

12 Marketing Ideas for Barber Shops That Actually Fill Chairs (2026)

# Marketing Ideas for Barber Shops

Last updated May 26, 2026 · By Rob P., Strategy

## Quick answer

The highest-return barber shop marketing is local and repeatable: a fully completed Google Business Profile, a steady flow of reviews, rebooking the next appointment before the client leaves the chair, and short video of your actual cuts. Paid ads work for barbershops, but only after those four are running.

## Key takeaways

*   Google Business Profile drives more new barbershop clients than any other channel, and it's free.
*   Rebooking at the chair is the single highest-return habit in the shop — it costs nothing and compounds weekly.
*   Before-and-after video outperforms every other content format for barbers, because the result is inherently visual.
*   Most barbershops don't need paid ads until the free channels are maxed out.
*   A client who visits every 3 weeks is worth roughly 17 cuts a year — retention beats acquisition on the maths.

## What's the fastest way to get more barbershop clients?

Fill out your Google Business Profile completely and start asking every satisfied client for a review. It's free, it takes an afternoon to set up, and for local search it outperforms everything else available to a barbershop.

When someone searches 'barber near me,' Google shows a map with three businesses. That local pack takes the overwhelming majority of clicks. Barbershops in it get walk-ins; barbershops below it mostly don't.

What actually moves you into it:

*   Claim and verify the profile. Unverified listings can't be optimised or posted to.
*   Correct primary category — 'Barber shop', not 'Hair salon'. They're different categories and they surface for different searches.
*   Every service listed with prices — fades, beard trims, hot towel shaves, kids' cuts, line-ups.
*   Real photos, updated monthly. Your actual shop, your actual work, your actual barbers. Not stock.
*   Accurate hours, including holidays.
*   Reviews, continuously. Volume and recency both count.

## How do you get barbershop clients to leave reviews?

Ask at the moment they're happiest — right after they see the finished cut in the mirror — and make it one tap.

The mistake is asking by email hours later, when the feeling has faded and the review is now a chore. In the chair, with the result visible, is when people actually agree.

What works in practice: a QR code at the station that opens your Google review form directly, a short text with the link sent while they're still paying, and the barber asking personally rather than a sign asking on their behalf. A named request from the person who just cut your hair converts several times better than a poster.

Consistency beats volume. Two reviews a week for a year is a stronger signal than forty in one month, which looks inorganic.

## What are the best barbershop marketing ideas that cost nothing?

Rebooking at the chair, referral cards, and getting your existing clients to bring people. These cost time rather than money and outperform most paid channels.

1\. Rebook before they leave. 'Same time in three weeks?' while they're paying. This is the highest-return sentence in the shop. A client on a standing three-week schedule is roughly 17 cuts a year; the same client rebooking whenever they remember might be 8.

2\. Referral cards that reward both people. '$5 off for you, $5 off for them.' Hand it to clients who already talk about the shop.

3\. Text your no-shows. Anyone who hasn't been in for six weeks gets one friendly message. A meaningful share come straight back — they didn't leave, they just forgot.

4\. Get on the booking apps properly. Booksy, Square Appointments, and Squire have their own internal search. A complete profile with photos and real availability gets surfaced inside apps people already have.

5\. Partner with neighbours. Gyms, tattoo shops, sneaker stores, barbers' natural adjacent audiences. Cross-promotion costs nothing and reaches the right people.

## What should barbershops post on social media?

Before-and-after video of real cuts, filmed on a phone, posted consistently. Barbering is one of the most visually satisfying trades there is, and short-form video is built for exactly that.

The format that works is simple and repeatable: client arrives, quick clip of the starting point, a few seconds of the work, the reveal. Fifteen to thirty seconds. Vertical. No production required.

Three things that raise the ceiling:

*   Always get permission before filming a client. Ask before the cut, not after.
*   Show the skill, not just the result. Fade blending and line work are the parts people find impressive.
*   Post the same clip to TikTok, Instagram Reels, and YouTube Shorts. One filming session, three platforms.

Tag your location on every post. Local discovery on these platforms genuinely works for barbershops, and it's the closest thing to free advertising available.

## Do Facebook and Instagram ads work for barbershops?

Yes, but only after the free channels are running, and only with tight geographic targeting. A barbershop's realistic catchment is a few miles.

Most barbershops that try paid ads and conclude they don't work made one of two mistakes: targeting too wide a radius, or sending clicks to a page with no way to book.

If you're going to run them:

| Setting | What works for a barbershop |
| --- | --- |
| Radius | 3–5 miles. People don't drive across town for a fade. |
| Objective | Bookings or messages — not traffic, not reach |
| Creative | Video of real cuts, your actual barbers |
| Offer | First-visit discount or a specific service |
| Destination | Direct to your booking app, not your homepage |
| Budget | Small and continuous beats large and occasional |

6\. A modest daily budget running continuously will outperform an occasional burst, because the platform needs steady data to optimise. For more on the mechanics, see our [Facebook ads](https://thinktankadagency.com/facebook-advertising) service page.

## How do barbershops get found by AI search?

By having complete, consistent business information across the web — the same details AI assistants read when someone asks for a barber recommendation in your area.

This is newer and most shops haven't touched it. When someone asks ChatGPT or Google's AI mode for a good barber in a neighbourhood, the answer gets assembled from sources the model can parse: your Google Business Profile, your reviews, directory listings, and any local coverage.

The practical version for a barbershop: make sure your name, address, and phone are identical everywhere they appear, keep your GBP services and hours current, and build up reviews that mention specific services. A review saying 'best skin fade in Highland Park' is a phrase an AI can match to a query in a way that a five-star rating alone cannot.
